Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
I work in renewable energy in Nigeria. Here is my simple and respectful suggestion for the final Scope 2 standard:

Please add a new “Emissions Impact” column next to the normal market-based method.

How it would work (very easy):

A company still buys normal certificates (EACs/RECs) and still reports zero in the usual market-based column — so the inventory stays honest and simple.
In the new “Emissions Impact” column, the company gets a higher score when the clean power they funded is built in a very dirty grid (like Nigeria’s) or in a place where many people have no electricity.
Example that every Nigerian understands:

Two big companies (Company A and Company B) both use the same amount of electricity worldwide and both buy 100 % clean certificates.

Company A buys only from Europe and America → normal “zero” in market-based method, small impact score.
Company B buys some certificates from new solar farms in Nigeria, Kenya, and Pakistan → also “zero” in market-based method (if you allow out-of-market purchases from dirty or low-access grids), but a much higher impact score because each megawatt-hour in Nigeria avoids 5–10 times more CO₂ and brings light to villages for the first time.
This small extra column will:

Keep the accounting strict and verified with certificates (no greenwashing)
Show the world who is really cutting the most CO₂ and helping the poorest communities
Send billions of dollars to African solar, wind, and mini-grids — exactly where the climate benefit is biggest
Reward ambition instead of punishing companies that want to do the most good
Africa causes less than 4 % of global emissions but has the cheapest sunshine and the biggest need. A simple “Emissions Impact” column will turn our sunshine into real climate credit and finally close the huge clean-energy finance gap on our continent.

Please give the companies that choose African projects a way to show the world: “We are doing more than just zero — we are doing the maximum good.”
